title: Wealth, earned and shared
hook: money is not evil; clinging to it and hoarding it are

segments.voice: Yesterday, work as worship: Lalo's bread and Bhago's feast, and kirat, honest work. Your line was work is worship. Which task did you do plainly and all the way through? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.

Is money bad? Ask that at a dinner table and watch it split. Somebody says money ruins everything it touches. Somebody else says try paying rent with good intentions. Both have a point, and both are a little stuck. Yesterday the Granth gave us honest work, and the bread it earns. But honest work, done well, sometimes earns more than bread. A shop does well. A farm has a good year. A salary goes up. Then the question isn't how to earn. It's what to do with what you've earned, and what it starts doing to you. Today's word is the thing on the table.
screen: `IS MONEY BAD?` → `THE TABLE SPLITS.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO WITH WHAT YOU EARN?`

segments.voice: First, money isn't the enemy. The salok we met yesterday honors the one who eats what they earn by their own work. Earning isn't shameful. Sikh life has room for farms, shops, businesses and savings; the householder needs a roof. Second, where the trouble starts. In Raag Asa, Guru Nanak looks at wealth with clear eyes, in hymns tradition links to Babar's invasion. In paraphrase: for the sake of this wealth, many were ruined and disgraced; it isn't piled up without wrongdoing, and it doesn't go along with anyone when they die. The problem isn't the coin. It's the clinging, the piling up, the wealth that has to be guarded and that guards you back. Third, the other half of yesterday's line. That same salok doesn't stop at earning. It says: and gives some of it from their hand. The hand that earns is meant to open. Sikhs call this sharing vand chhakna, and tradition adds a practice called dasvandh, setting aside a tenth share of what you earn for the community and for those in need. Gifts like this can help feed the langar. Fourth, why the two belong together. Earning without sharing tightens the fist. Sharing without honest earning gives away what was never yours. Put together, money becomes something that moves through a life instead of sitting on it. A hand that earns and then opens is a hand that isn't owned by what it holds. Earned and shared.
screen: `EARNING IS NOT SHAMEFUL.` · `IT DOESN'T GO ALONG AT DEATH.` · `THE HAND THAT EARNS SHOULD OPEN.` · `MONEY MOVES THROUGH, NOT SITS ON.` · then, large: `EARNED AND SHARED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share some money. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind what you earned or received this week. Don't add it up. Just hold the picture. Then think of one place it could go that isn't you: a food bank, a gurdwara's langar, a neighbor who's short this month, a cause you care about. The amount doesn't matter. Even a small sum counts. Hold your hand open on your lap while you breathe, and notice what it feels like to plan to let go of something. If you pray, you can hold the gift with Waheguru. After the bell, give it. The bell holds the time.
Wealth. Not evil in itself; earned honestly, it is meant to be shared, and it does not go along with anyone at the end. Today's word.
Your line: earned and shared. Today, give a little of what you earned to someone else, quietly, from your own hand. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of vand chhakna, sharing what one earns, and tradition describes dasvandh, setting aside a share of income, for the community and those in need, including the langar.
